title: Law & Your Rights · Episode 1
chapters: Common law and civil law: the world's two great legal families
Trial by jury: twelve ordinary people
Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish

units.t: Law & Your Rights. Episode one.
In this episode: How Australian law works, Common law and civil law: the world's two great legal families, Trial by jury: twelve ordinary people and Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish.
Part one. How Australian law works.
Every day you live inside a system of rules built over 800 years, from English judges to the High Court in Canberra.
Here's how it actually fits together.
Statute and common law.
Australian law has two main sources.
Legislation is Acts passed by the Commonwealth, state and territory parliaments, such as road rules or the Fair Work Act.
Common law is the body of principles built up by judges deciding cases over centuries, inherited from England in 1788.
Where the two clash, legislation generally wins, because parliament can override the common law within the limits of the Constitution.
The common law runs on precedent.
The core reasoning in a decision becomes a rule that lower courts in the same system must follow in similar cases.
That makes law predictable, yet lets it evolve.
Donoghue v Stevenson, 1932, a Scottish case about a snail in a ginger beer bottle, shaped the law of negligence across the common law world, including Australia.
Layers and ladders.
Australia is a federation, so there is no single set of laws.
The Commonwealth makes laws on national subjects like tax, defence, immigration and trade.
The six states, and the ACT and Northern Territory, make most everyday laws, including most crimes, driving, property, schools and hospitals.
That is why penalties, or the rules for renting a home, can differ between Sydney and Perth.
Courts form a ladder.
Local or Magistrates Courts handle most criminal cases and smaller civil claims.
District Courts, the County Court in Victoria, hear more serious crimes and larger claims.
Supreme Courts hear the gravest cases, such as murder, plus appeals.
Federal courts include the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court.
Criminal versus civil.
In a criminal case, the state prosecutes someone for breaking the law, which is why cases are named like R v Smith, with R for the Crown.
Penalties include fines, community orders and prison.
The prosecution must prove every element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
The accused is presumed innocent and doesn't have to prove anything.
In a civil case, one party, the plaintiff, sues another, the defendant, usually for money called damages.
The standard is lower: the balance of probabilities, meaning more likely than not.
One event, such as a car crash, can lead to both kinds of case.
Fair trials and juries.
Australian trials are adversarial: two sides present their cases while the judge acts as a neutral umpire.
Accused people generally have a right to silence, so refusing to answer police questions usually can't be used as evidence of guilt, though some laws create exceptions.
In Dietrich v The Queen, 1992, the High Court held that a serious trial may be delayed if an accused who can't afford a lawyer would otherwise face an unfair trial.
Serious criminal trials are usually heard by a jury, typically 12 people chosen at random from the electoral roll.
The jury decides the facts and guilt.
The judge rules on the law and sets the sentence.
For serious Commonwealth offences, the High Court has held jury verdicts must be unanimous.
Juries are rare in civil cases.
The High Court and help.
The High Court of Australia, created by the Constitution and first sitting in 1903, sits at the top.
Its seven justices, based in Canberra, decide appeals from every other court and settle disputes about the Constitution.
Appeals usually need special leave, so only important cases are heard.
Since the Australia Act 1986, no appeals can go to Britain's Privy Council.
Its decisions can reshape the nation: in Mabo, 1992, it rejected the idea that Australia was 'terra nullius'.
This lesson is general information only.
If you have a legal problem, Legal Aid and community legal centres offer free or low-cost help, and a lawyer can advise on your situation.
The key idea: Australian law comes from parliaments, legislation, and judges' decisions, common law, and judges follow precedent.
Part two. Common law and civil law: the world's two great legal families.
Most of the world's legal systems descend from one of two ancestors: medieval English judges, or the law books of ancient Rome.
Which one you live under shapes how courts work.
Two family trees.
Arrested in Sydney, Paris, Tokyo or Chicago, you would meet courtrooms that work differently.
Much of the difference is history.
Common law grew from medieval England and spread with the British Empire, to Australia, the United States, Canada, New Zealand and India.
Civil law grew from Roman law, revived in medieval Europe and organised into national codes.
It covers most of continental Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa, so by number of countries it is more widespread.
Beware the vocabulary.
In everyday Australian use, civil law means non-criminal disputes, such as contracts and negligence.
Here it names a whole tradition built on written codes, and civil law countries have criminal cases too.
Lawyers often say 'civilian systems' for clarity.
Judges on horseback.
After the Norman conquest of 1066, English kings gradually built a national system of royal courts.
Under Henry II, who reigned from 1154 to 1189, royal judges travelled on circuits around the country, hearing cases in the king's name.
Over time they developed rules that applied across the whole realm, a law common to all of England, which is where the name comes from.
Rather than starting from a grand written code, the common law grew case by case.
Judges looked at how earlier cases had been decided and followed them.
This principle, called precedent, means a decision of a higher court binds lower courts in similar cases.
Parliament can override judge-made law with statutes, but much of the law began in courtrooms.
Rome's second life.
In the 530s, the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian ordered his lawyers to collect and organise centuries of Roman law.
The result, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, or Body of Civil Law, was a vast compilation of legal rules and expert opinions.
For centuries it was largely forgotten in Western Europe.
Then, in the late 1000s, scholars in Bologna, Italy, began studying it closely, and Roman law became the basis of university legal education across Europe.
Many centuries later, nations turned these ideas into tidy national codes.
The most influential was France's Civil Code of 1804, often called the Napoleonic Code.
Germany's Civil Code of 1900 was another giant, later influencing countries as different as Japan and Greece.
Inside the courtroom.
The traditions also differ in how trials work.
Common law systems are usually adversarial.
Two sides, each with its own lawyers, present evidence and question witnesses, while a judge acts like an umpire and, in serious criminal cases, a jury often decides the facts.
Civil law systems are usually more inquisitorial.
Judges, sometimes including an investigating judge before trial, take a more active role in gathering evidence and questioning witnesses, and written files matter more.
Juries are less common, although some countries use lay judges who sit alongside professionals.
Judges in civil law countries are often career officials trained for the role, rather than experienced lawyers appointed later in life, as is common in Australia.
Blended and borrowed.
Real legal systems are rarely pure.
Scotland and South Africa have mixed systems combining civil law roots with common law influences.
In Canada, Quebec uses a civil code for private law, while the other provinces follow common law.
Louisiana's private law shows its French and Spanish heritage.
Many countries also blend in religious or customary law.
The two great families have also drifted closer.
Common law countries now rely on huge volumes of statutes, so much of their law is written down much like a code.
Meanwhile, courts in civil law countries often follow earlier decisions of higher courts in practice, even where they are not formally bound.
Two old family trees, with branches increasingly intertwined.
The key idea: Most legal systems descend from either the common law or the civil law tradition, and 'civil law' has two meanings.
Part three. Trial by jury: twelve ordinary people.
Somewhere in Australia today, twelve strangers are sitting in a small room deciding whether someone is guilty of a serious crime.
Why do we hand such power to ordinary citizens, and what actually happens if your name is drawn?
Called by chance.
An envelope from the sheriff's office or court tells you that you have been selected for possible jury service.
It is a normal part of being enrolled to vote: in every state and territory, potential jurors are chosen at random from the electoral roll.
Not everyone summoned serves.
Some people are ineligible, such as many lawyers, police officers and politicians, and others can be excused for good reasons, like caring duties or serious hardship.
Respond by the deadline, because ignoring a summons can lead to a fine.
Employers generally cannot penalise you for serving, and jurors receive an allowance, though amounts and wage top-ups vary by state.
This is general information, not legal advice, so check your state or territory court's juror pages.
From ordeals to juries.
In early medieval England, guilt could be tested by ordeal: carrying a red-hot iron or being lowered into water, with the outcome believed to reveal God's judgment.
In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council banned priests from taking part, which made ordeals unworkable.
Courts turned to groups of local men already asked about crimes in their area, who gradually became neutral judges of evidence.
In 1670 the jury trying Quakers William Penn and William Mead refused to convict, even after the judge locked the jurors up and fined them.
Juror Edward Bushel challenged his imprisonment.
In Bushel's Case, Sir John Vaughan ruled that jurors cannot be punished for a verdict the judge dislikes.
The principle travelled with English law to Australia.
Juries in Australia.
Most legal matters in Australia do not involve a jury.
Minor offences and most civil disputes, such as contract claims, are decided by a magistrate or judge alone.
Juries mainly decide serious criminal cases, such as murder, sexual offences, serious assault and large-scale fraud, and criminal juries usually have twelve members.
Section 80 of the Constitution says a trial on indictment for a Commonwealth offence must be by jury, though the High Court has read that protection fairly narrowly.
In some states an accused person can choose a judge-alone trial in certain circumstances.
Civil juries are rare, but some states still allow them in particular cases, such as some defamation claims.
Inside the jury room.
The judge controls the courtroom, rules on evidence and explains the law.
The jury decides what actually happened.
In a criminal case, jurors must be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt, a high standard designed to protect innocent people from wrongful conviction.
They must decide only on evidence presented in court.
Doing your own research, searching online about the case or visiting the scene can be a criminal offence, because it can lead to an unfair trial.
Jury room discussions stay confidential even after the case ends.
Verdicts traditionally had to be unanimous, but most states now allow majority verdicts in some circumstances after long deliberation.
Some trials involve distressing evidence, and courts in most states offer free, confidential counselling to jurors afterwards.
The case for and against.
Supporters say juries bring community values into the courtroom and check the power of the state, since a government cannot imprison someone for a serious crime without convincing ordinary citizens.
Juries also spread responsibility for grave decisions across many people and give citizens a direct role in justice.
Many jurors find the experience absorbing and meaningful.
Critics raise real concerns.
Complex fraud or scientific evidence can be hard for non-experts to follow, jury trials take longer and cost more, and jurors may be swayed by media coverage or personal impressions.
Some countries, such as Japan, use mixed panels of judges and citizens instead.
Most Australian legal experts accept the system is imperfect, and debate about how to improve it continues.
The key idea: Jurors are drawn at random from the electoral roll, and answering a summons is a legal duty.
Part four. Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish.
Two Latin words protect you from being locked away without reason.
They have stood up to kings, slave owners and presidents.
Produce the body.
Habeas corpus is Latin for 'you shall have the body'.
It is the name of a writ, a formal court order, directed at whoever is holding a prisoner, whether a jailer, a soldier or a government official.
The writ commands them to bring the person before the court and show a lawful reason for the detention.
If they cannot, the judge can order the prisoner released.
It does not decide whether someone is guilty.
It asks a more basic question: is there any legal authority to hold this person at all?
That makes it a check on power itself.
Without it, a government could make people disappear into cells with no charge, no trial and no end date.
Forged by conflict.
Versions of the writ existed in English courts by the 1200s, at first mostly to bring people to court.
Judges later used it to test whether detentions were lawful, drawing strength from Magna Carta of 1215: no free man to be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.
In 1627 Charles I jailed knights who refused a forced loan demanded without Parliament's consent.
The jailer's only answer was that they were held by the king's special command, and the court refused to release them.
Outrage helped produce the Petition of Right in 1628, declaring such imprisonment unlawful.
In 1679 Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, setting deadlines and penalties to stop officials dodging the writ.
James Somerset's freedom.
In 1772 the writ was used in a dramatic case.
James Somerset had been enslaved in Virginia and brought to England by Charles Stewart, a customs official.
Somerset escaped, was recaptured and was put aboard a ship bound for Jamaica, where he would be sold.
Supporters, including the campaigner Granville Sharp, sought habeas corpus.
Lord Mansfield, the senior judge of the King's Bench, ruled that no law in England allowed a master to force Somerset out of the country, and Somerset was freed.
The decision did not abolish slavery, which continued in British colonies for decades.
But it was widely celebrated and became a landmark in the long struggle against slavery.
Suspending the writ.
Because habeas corpus limits government power, governments under pressure have sometimes tried to switch it off.
Britain's Parliament suspended it several times, for example in the 1790s amid fears of revolution spreading from France.
The framers of the United States Constitution included the writ but allowed suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety required it.
In 1861, at the start of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln suspended it in some areas.
Chief Justice Roger Taney argued in the Merryman case that only Congress had that power, and Lincoln largely ignored him.
Congress later authorised suspension.
Lawyers and historians still debate how far emergencies justify setting aside this ancient safeguard.
The writ today.
English colonists carried habeas corpus around the world.
It remains part of the law in countries including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and the United States.
In Australia, superior courts such as the state Supreme Courts and the High Court can issue it.
In practice, many detentions are now reviewed through other routes, such as bail hearings, appeals and judicial review, so the old writ is used less often than its fame suggests.
But it still matters most when other protections fail.
It has been invoked over immigration detention, mental health detention and wartime imprisonment.
Its message endures: power must always answer one question in court.
By what lawful authority is this person being held?
The key idea: Habeas corpus is a court order demanding that a jailer justify why a person is being held.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the principle of precedent require of a lower court?
Answer. Follow earlier decisions of higher courts in similar cases.
Question two. What does 'civil law' mean in the phrase 'civil law tradition'?
Answer. A legal tradition built on Roman law and written codes.
Question three. Where do Australian courts draw potential jurors from?
Answer. The electoral roll.
Question four. What question does habeas corpus force a jailer to answer?
Answer. What lawful authority justifies the detention.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
